chapter: Small groups, Europe and Kansas City memories (repeated passages)
title: Basie's piano restraint and too many riffs behind a soloist
summary: Basie and Duke left space for soloists; Dickenson dislikes heavy background rhythm and riffs that crowd the soloist.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: because I was playing with some of the guys that were really great, you know. Yeah, there were lots of greats in there that are still alive, you know. Great players, you know. It was a great band, you know. And Basie played an odd piano, and it sounded good -- it fitted. He didn't overload the sounds, you know. Sometimes a guy can play too much piano, and it drowns out everything, you know. He's playing his solo while you're playing your solo. That's no good. Basie just DING-DING, you know, that...and let you go ahead by yourself. And that's a good style, a very good band style. Duke had that style, you know. And that's a great band style for a pianist, you know, not to drown out the man that's playing the solo.

That's why a lot of times I don't like a background rhythm behind me, because it takes away from what I think of what I am going to do, you know. It takes something away from my mind. I have to go follow their pattern then, you know. Otherwise, I don't get to form my own thoughts. You know, like guys play rhythm lines like [SINGS BROKEN BOPPISSH RHYTHM]. Well, you have to play in between that. You really ain't playing a solo. You're just doing the fill-ins. You understand what I mean?
Yeah, sure. Sure. That's why a lot of guys don't like no background, too much background. Whole notes is all right. But outside of that...
You mean riffing can get to be too much...

You can put too many riffs in a thing. If you just go DUT-DUT or something like that... But if you can go DUT-DE-DA, DE-DUT-DE-DA, you only give them about two... You give them half a measure to play, and between that, while you're doing DUT-DE-DU, DE-DUT-DE-DU, you've got one beat in between there. Really one beat. And it means you've got to play in between that. Because you said, DUT-DE-DU, DE-DUT-DE-DU, then you're drowning out what he's playing anyhow! So there's no use for him to do nothin' but just do the little fill-in. But nobody understands that. They think that you have to do that. That's all right for the out chorus, you know, or something like that, if you're going to put a whole lot of riffs in it. It's all right to put just a little, fill in between what the guy is playing, what the soloist is playing.
Well, that way you sort of help him rather than...
Yeah, instead of you're restricting him.
You know who I always thought was really a master at setting riffs, was Lips.
He used to do that on sessions, and...

Yes. Well, it's got to be a good riff. You understand what I mean? If you're putting too much figuration in a thing, you spoil the man's ideas. That's not only... Don't take my word as the prayer book.
